lead: Filtering in the frequency domain means changing an image by multiplying its DFT by a mask H(u,v). The mask keeps some frequencies and kills others. A low-pass mask keeps the centre, so noise and fine detail go and the picture blurs. A high-pass mask does the reverse, and edges survive. This is used for denoising, for removing periodic scan lines from a scanned page, and for flattening uneven lighting in a photograph. This chapter gives the pipeline, the three standard low-pass shapes and their high-pass partners.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.6 — the DFT pair, separability and the convolution theorem.

blocks.text: In space, a filter is a convolution with a mask (see 2.3). In frequency, the same filter is a single multiplication, because convolution in space equals multiplication in frequency. That is the convolution theorem from Chapter 2.6.

blocks.where: f(x,y) is the input image; F(u,v) is its DFT; H(u,v) is the transfer function, a mask of the same size; the dot is a pixel-by-pixel multiply at every (u,v); IDFT is the inverse discrete Fourier transform; Re takes the real part; g(x,y) is the filtered image.

items: Centre the spectrum: multiply f(x,y) by (−1)^(x+y) before the DFT, or shift the spectrum after it.
Build H(u,v) of the same size, usually from the distance D(u,v).
Multiply: G(u,v) = H(u,v) · F(u,v) at every point.
Inverse FFT to return to space.
Take the real part and clip to 0–255.

blocks.text: The FFT is what makes this practical. For an N×N image the direct DFT costs about N⁴ operations and the 2-D FFT about N² log₂ N. At N = 1024 that is roughly 10⁵ times fewer operations, so a full-image frequency filter runs in a fraction of a second on a laptop. Once F is in memory, applying H is only N² complex multiplies — cheaper than one pass of a 3×3 spatial mask.

sections.h3: Distance D(u,v) and the ideal low-pass

blocks.text: The raw DFT puts zero frequency at pixel (0,0). A radial filter wants it in the middle, so the spectrum is centred first. Distance from the centre is D(u,v) = √(u² + v²), where u and v are counted from the centre pixel of the M×N spectrum. D is measured in spectrum pixels, not in hertz.
A filter written as H(D) depends only on distance, so it is circularly symmetric: it treats horizontal and vertical detail alike. The radius D₀ is the cutoff.
H_ideal(D) = 1 for D ≤ D₀, and 0 for D > D₀
blocks.where: D₀ is the cutoff radius in spectrum pixels; every frequency inside the circle of radius D₀ passes unchanged, everything outside is set to zero.

blocks.text: The ideal filter is the sharpest possible cut, and that is its problem. A step in H has a sinc-shaped inverse transform, so the output shows ripples around every edge. This is ringing, and it gets worse as D₀ shrinks. Sharpening the cutoff sharpens the ripples too.
The Butterworth filter softens the step.

blocks.where: n is the order, a positive number that sets how sharp the knee is; D₀ is the cutoff radius; D is the distance from the centre. At D = D₀ the ratio is 1, so H = 1/2 for every order — a fixed half-power point.

blocks.text: Small n gives a gentle roll-off and almost no ringing. As n grows, the curve approaches the ideal step and ringing comes back. Order 2 is a common compromise.
The Gaussian filter has no order at all.

blocks.where: D₀ sets the width of the passband (not a hard cutoff); D is the distance from the centre; e ≈ 2.718. At D = D₀, H = e^(−0.5) = 0.607, and at D = 2D₀, H = e^(−2) = 0.135.

blocks.text: The inverse transform of a Gaussian is another Gaussian, which has no side lobes. So the equivalent spatial mask is smooth, and a Gaussian low-pass never rings. That is why it is the default choice for smoothing in the frequency domain.

Every low-pass has a high-pass partner: H_hp(u,v) = 1 − H_lp(u,v). Whatever the low-pass removed, the high-pass keeps. A Gaussian high-pass is 1 − e^(−D²/2D₀²): zero at the centre, tending to 1 far out. This is the frequency-domain form of the sharpening in 2.5 — edges and texture survive, flat regions go grey.

Selective filters kill narrow bands instead of whole regions. A band-reject mask sets H = 0 on a ring of radii; a notch sets H = 0 in small spots. The usual target is periodic noise — scan lines, a striped shirt, mains hum — which shows up as bright spikes away from the centre. Because the DFT of a real image is conjugate symmetric, F(u,v) = F*(M−u, N−v), a notch at (u₀,v₀) must be repeated at (M−u₀, N−v₀).

For uneven lighting, take logs first: log f = log i + log r, where i is the illumination (slowly varying, low frequency) and r is the reflectance (the object's detail, high frequency). Low-pass the log to estimate i, subtract it, then exponentiate. This is homomorphic filtering; it removes a shadow gradient without destroying contrast. Unit 3 takes periodic-noise removal further.

figure.caption: With D₀ = 50, at D = 50 the ideal mask passes 1, Butterworth order 2 passes 0.5 and Gaussian 0.607; at D = 100 they pass 0, 0.0588 and 0.135. Only the ideal mask has a step, so only it rings.

spec.aria: H against distance D from 0 to 150 for three low-pass masks: the ideal step falling from 1 to 0 at D = 50, the Butterworth curve through 0.5 at 50, and the Gaussian through 0.607 at 50. Dots at D = 50 and 100, and a table of the six values.

examples.question: A 256×256 grayscale image is filtered in the frequency domain with a centred spectrum. The cutoff is D₀ = 50 spectrum pixels. Find the transfer function H at the two radii D = 50 and D = 100 for (a) an ideal low-pass filter, (b) a Butterworth low-pass of order n = 2, (c) a Gaussian low-pass with the same D₀. State which one rings.
steps: Ideal filter: H = 1 when D ≤ D₀ and 0 otherwise. At D = 50 the point lies exactly on the boundary, so take the inside value, H = 1. At D = 100 > 50, H = 0.
Butterworth, exponent 2n = 4. At D = 50: (50/50)⁴ = 1, so H = 1/(1+1) = 0.5. This is the half-power point, true for any order.
Gaussian. Exponent is −D²/(2D₀²) = −2500/5000 = −0.5 at D = 50, so H = e^(−0.5) = 0.607.
Gaussian at D = 100: −10000/5000 = −2, so H = e^(−2) = 0.135. The Gaussian roll-off is gentler than Butterworth order 2 at the same D₀.
Ringing comes from a sharp step in H. Only the ideal filter has one, so only (a) rings; the Gaussian never does.
examples.answer: At D = 50 the three filters give H = 1, 0.5 and 0.607; at D = 100 they give H = 0, 0.0588 and 0.135, and only the ideal filter rings.

examples.question: A Butterworth low-pass has D₀ = 100 pixels and order n = 3. Compute H at D = 100 and at D = 200.

traps: Forgetting the real part after the inverse DFT. The spectrum of a real image is conjugate symmetric, so the result is real in theory, but floating point leaves a tiny imaginary residue; passing a complex array to an 8-bit display gives a wrong image.
Forgetting to centre the spectrum. With the origin at the corner, D = √(u²+v²) places the passband at a corner instead of the middle, so the wrong frequencies are kept.
Swapping D₀ and n. D₀ is a radius in spectrum pixels and controls the size of the passband; n is the Butterworth order and controls the sharpness of the knee.

Assuming the ideal filter is the best one. It is the sharpest cut and the worst ringer; the expected answer is usually that the Gaussian has no ringing because its inverse transform has no side lobes.
Placing a single notch. A notch at (u₀,v₀) must be duplicated at (M−u₀, N−v₀), otherwise the output is not real.

quiz.q: What does multiplying F(u,v) by H(u,v) correspond to in the spatial domain?
quiz.a: A convolution of the image with the inverse transform of H, that is, a linear filter. Multiplication in frequency equals convolution in space.

quiz.q: Why does a Gaussian low-pass filter not produce ringing?
quiz.a: Its inverse transform is another Gaussian, which has no side lobes. Ringing comes from a sharp step in H, whose inverse transform is a sinc with large side lobes.

quiz.q: Why must the spectrum be centred before a radial mask is applied?
quiz.a: The raw DFT puts zero frequency at pixel (0,0). A mask built from D = √(u²+v²) assumes the origin is at the centre, so without centring the mask lands in the wrong place.

quiz.q: A Butterworth low-pass has D₀ = 100 pixels and order n = 3. Find H at D = 100 and D = 200.
A Gaussian high-pass has D₀ = 40 pixels. Find H at D = 40 pixels.
quiz.a: H_hp = 1 − e^(−D²/2D₀²). At D = D₀ the exponent is −0.5, so H = 1 − 0.607 = 0.393.

quiz.q: A scanned page shows faint diagonal stripes. Which frequency-domain step removes them, and why?
quiz.a: Notch (or band-reject) filtering. Periodic stripes put a pair of bright spikes at fixed positions away from the centre; zero those spikes and their conjugate points and the rest of the image is untouched.

quiz.q: Why does a smaller D₀ in an ideal low-pass give stronger ringing?
quiz.a: A smaller D₀ means a narrower passband, that is, a sharper step in H. The sinc side lobes of the inverse transform spread wider in space, so the ripples around each edge grow.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same multiply-by-a-mask pipeline runs in modern computational photography: deconvolution on phone cameras, ring-artefact removal in CT reconstruction, and FFT-based convolution inside neural networks once kernels get large. An optical system is described by its modulation transfer function, which is exactly an H(u,v) measured with a test chart. Read a 2-D log-magnitude spectrum fluently and most periodic-noise problems become visible at a glance. Search for Butterworth versus Gaussian low-pass ringing, and for homomorphic filtering of illumination and reflectance, to go further.
